title: Spiritual gifts in service
summary: God equips every believer for service. The Spirit distributes different gifts, and one body - the Church - joins them into a whole. Everyone is to discover and use their gift. The Bible also gives criteria for recognizing a true gift and a true prophet. The gift of healing reminds us that God acts today - within His will and the mystery of suffering. The goal of all the gifts: building up the Church.

items.comment: Different gifts, different ministries - but "the same Spirit" and "the same God." To each is given "the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good." No one is left out.

questions.text: What does it mean that you receive a gift not for yourself, but "for the common good"?

items.comment: It is the Spirit who "distributes to each one as He wills." A gift is not a reward for merit nor a reason for pride - it is a gift, that is, something received.

questions.text: Since it is the Spirit who chooses and distributes the gifts, what does that say about comparing ourselves with others?

items.comment: "As good stewards... serve one another" with the gift each has received. A gift is an entrusted treasure to be used, not hidden away.

questions.text: How does a "steward of a gift" differ from an "owner of a talent"?

items.label: "gifts of grace" (charismata)
items.content: The Greek *charisma* (plural *charismata*, 1 Cor 12; Rom 12) comes from *charis* - "grace." Spiritual gifts are by definition "expressions of grace": something received freely, not earned. The very word rules out pride and comparison - a gift is not a medal, but equipment for service.

questions.text: How does the link *charisma-charis* (gift-grace) guard against two extremes: pride and a sense of worthlessness?

items.label: two words: "spiritual" and "gifts"
items.content: Paul opens his discussion with the word *pneumatika* - "spiritual things" (1 Cor 12:1), but almost immediately switches to *charismata* - "gifts of grace" (1 Cor 12:4). Commentators suggest that *pneumatika* was the Corinthians' own term, with which they stressed their own "spirituality"; Paul deliberately changes the word to shift the emphasis from experience to the grace of the Giver and to service.

questions.text: What changes in our view when we call a "spiritual gift" first a "gift of grace" and not "my spiritual experience"?

items.comment: Just as a body has many members with different functions, so does the Church. The gifts listed (serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, mercy) are ordinary and practical - most of us already carry them within us.

questions.text: Which of the gifts listed sounds closest to what comes naturally to you?

items.comment: The foot is not inferior to the hand, nor the ear to the eye. If the whole body were an eye - there would be no body. Diversity is not a problem to be evened out, but God's design.

questions.text: When have you felt "less important" in your community? How does this picture of the body answer that?

items.label: "no gift is worth less"
items.content: The image of the body (1 Cor 12; Rom 12) serves Paul to show that the gifts complement one another and none is superfluous. When those regarded as the "least" are missing, the whole body suffers. As one commentary puts it: "none of the gifts of grace is worthless, and none is worth less than another" - a hierarchy of importance is foreign to Paul's thought.

items.comment: "I have no need of you" - no member is superfluous, and the weaker ones are cared for all the more. When one suffers, all suffer; when one is honored, all rejoice.

questions.text: What would it mean in your community to treat the "weaker" ones with more care, not less?

items.comment: Christ gave the Church different ministries "to equip the saints for the work of ministry." The goal: the maturity and unity of the whole body - so that everyone can serve, not only the leaders.

questions.text: According to this text, what is the true purpose of having leaders and teachers in the Church?

items.label: different lists of gifts in the New Testament
items.content: The lists of gifts (1 Cor 12:8-10, 28; Rom 12:6-8; Eph 4:11; 1 Pet 4:11) differ from one another and partly overlap. This indicates that none of them is a closed catalog - the Spirit equips the Church according to need, and the goal is always to build up the body, not the spectacular nature of a gift.

items.label: "charismatic" means "gifted for service"
items.content: In the New Testament the whole Church is "charismatic," because the whole Church has been gifted for mission. Today the word brings to mind an emotional experience during a worship service, but in the biblical sense "charismatic" simply means "equipped for service" - personally and as a community (Acts 1:8; 4:31).

questions.text: How does the picture of the Church change when we understand "charismatic" as "gifted for service" rather than "expressive in experience"?

items.comment: The master distributes talents "to each according to his ability." Two servants multiply them, the third buries his. An unused gift withers - it was given to be put to work.

questions.text: What most often makes people "bury" their gift instead of using it?

items.comment: "Do not neglect the gift that is in you." A gift is sometimes noticed and confirmed by the community - it is worth nurturing, not suppressing.

questions.text: Who in your life could help you recognize a gift you do not see in yourself?

items.comment: Paul urges us to "fan into flame" the gift of God, for God gave "a spirit of power, love, and sound judgment," not of fear. Often it is fear that quenches a gift.

questions.text: What gift in you needs to be "fanned into flame" today - and what is dampening it in you?

items.label: first the Giver, then the gifts
items.content: The Acts of the Apostles uses the word *dorea* ("gift") for the Holy Spirit Himself, given to believers (Acts 2:38; 10:45; 11:17). The order is significant: first comes the Giver - the Spirit - and only then do the *charismata*, the individual gifts, appear (1 Cor 12). Seeking a gift therefore begins with openness to the Spirit Himself, not with hunting for a particular ability.

questions.text: How does the search for "your gift" change when you first ask for the Giver Himself, and not for a particular skill?

items.comment: "To the Law and to the testimony!" - if anyone speaks otherwise than the Word, there is no light in him. The first criterion of a true gift: agreement with Scripture.

questions.text: Why must agreement with the Bible be the first test of every "inspired" message?

items.comment: "By their fruits you will know them." A true gift and a true prophet are known not by how impressive they are, but by the fruits of their life and teaching.

questions.text: What "fruits" distinguish authentic service from a mere appearance of it?

items.comment: "Test the spirits, whether they are from God." Discernment is neither a lack of faith nor suspicion - it is a biblical duty, for "many false prophets have gone out into the world."

questions.text: How does healthy "testing of the spirits" differ from gullibility and from cynical suspicion?

items.label: criteria for discerning a true prophet
items.content: The Bible gives a coherent set of tests: agreement with Scripture (Isa 8:20), the fulfillment of what was foretold (Deut 18:21-22), the fruits of life and teaching (Matt 7:15-20), and the confession of Christ come in the flesh (1 John 4:2-3). These are objective criteria - they do not depend on the impressions or charisma of the speaker. (The gift of prophecy as a special mark of the remnant is the subject of a separate study, study 26; here we treat it in general, without reference to Ellen White.)

items.label: "the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy"
items.content: In Rev 19:10 the angel speaks of those "who hold the testimony of Jesus," and John explains: "the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy." In Greek *tēn martyrian Iēsou* is a "subjective" genitive - a testimony coming FROM Jesus. In Rev 22:9 the same angel, instead of "the testimony of Jesus," says "the prophets," which shows that both expressions are connected with the gift of prophecy. (The connection of this gift with the remnant people is developed in study 26.)

items.comment: The test of a prophet is the fulfillment of his words. God Himself gives the criterion - truth defends itself, it does not fear verification.

questions.text: What does it tell us about God that He allows, and even commands, us to test those who speak in His name?

items.label: conditional prophecy (Nineveh)
items.content: The test of Deut 18:22 must be read together with the principle of conditional prophecy (Jer 18:7-10). Jonah proclaimed: "forty more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown" - and the city was not overthrown, because it repented. Jonah remained a true prophet nonetheless: an announcement of judgment contains a hidden condition, and its non-fulfillment after repentance does not make the prophet false.

questions.text: Why does the repentance of Nineveh not undermine God's test of a prophet in Deut 18:22, but rather complete it?

items.comment: "Do not quench the Spirit... test everything; hold fast what is good." The balance: openness to the working of the Spirit together with discernment.

questions.text: How can you keep the balance between "do not quench the Spirit" and "test everything"?

sections.heading: The gift of healing and God's action today

items.comment: The sick person is to call the elders to pray over him and anoint him with oil; "the prayer of faith will save the sick." God invites us to bring our illnesses to Him - prayer for healing is a normal part of the life of the Church.

questions.text: What holds you back from asking the community for prayer when you are ill - and what does this text say about that?

items.comment: Among the gifts of the Spirit are also "gifts of healing" and "the working of miracles." God acts today - healing is a gift of the Spirit, not just an old story.

questions.text: Why do you think healing is called a "gift" here, and not a "reward" or a "right"?

items.label: the gift of healing: the ordinary way and the exceptions
items.content: Paul speaks of "gifts of healing" in the plural (1 Cor 12:9). The ordinary way of seeking healing that God points to is prayer and anointing with oil (Jas 5:14-15), though healing is sometimes granted through prayer alone. "The working of miracles" (1 Cor 12:10) is connected with the gift of healing, but is broader - it includes what humanly seems impossible.

questions.text: Why is it good that the Bible gives an "ordinary way" (prayer and anointing) and yet does not close off other ways for God to act?

items.comment: Paul asked three times for healing, but heard: "My grace is sufficient for you." God does not always heal at once, and not always as we ask - His power also works in weakness. This is the mystery of suffering, not a lack of God's love.

questions.text: How can you reconcile faith in healing with the fact that sometimes God says "My grace is sufficient for you"?

items.comment: Jesus rejects the simple formula "illness = punishment for sin." Suffering remains a mystery, yet in it "the works of God may be displayed."

questions.text: What changes in how you view suffering when you reject the thinking "I am ill because I have done wrong"?

application.text: God does not divide believers into "professionals" and "spectators." The Spirit equips everyone for service and gives at least one gift - for the common good. Your gift is needed by the body of Christ: without you something is missing. It is worth discovering it (often with the community's help) and using it, rather than burying it out of fear. The Bible also teaches wise discernment of true gifts and prophets - always according to the Word and the fruits. And when we are ill, we can boldly ask for prayer for healing, trusting that God acts today - even if His answer is sometimes a mystery, and His grace is sufficient also in weakness.
application.challenge: This week ask two people who know you: "What gift or strength do you see in me?" Choose one way to use that gift soon in serving someone specific. If you are struggling with illness - ask the community or the elders for prayer (Jas 5:14).
